title: The Fish Rots from the Head Down
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele argues that teachers should stop covering for unsustainable, policy-driven workload with personal martyrdom and instead adopt five evidence-informed habits that protect their time and energy. He opens with the proverb that the fish rots from the head down, locating the problem in shifting policy, accountability metrics and top-down initiatives rather than in individual teachers. Each of the five shifts is paired with a research anchor (cognitive load theory, Rosenshine, Coe and colleagues, Sweller and Tricot, decision fatigue) and a concrete step to take the next morning. The shifts are to keep lesson structure consistent and simple, adapt existing resources and let AI handle formatting, prefer four good-enough lessons to one perfect one, resist curriculum bloat, and triage energy on duties outside the classroom. His conclusion is that excellence comes from clarity, simple structure and a rested teacher, not from laminated perfection.
points: A fixed lesson spine (retrieval starter, I do, We do, You do) lowers extraneous cognitive load for students and planning load for the teacher, so new ingredients should be added only when their time cost is known.
Adapting a trusted shared deck in about ten minutes and using AI as a formatting assistant frees energy for rehearsing explanations, which is where a teacher's real value lies.

A hard evening stop time and four good-enough lessons beat one masterpiece, because sleep deprivation degrades the executive functioning teaching depends on; a flawed slide can even become a spot-the-mistake task.
Holding the line on whole-school initiatives means auditing lesson minutes and justifying trade-offs in cognitive-load terms, while duty time follows a 'safety first, details second' rule.
quotes: There is an old proverb that every seasoned educator eventually comes to understand: the fish rots from the head down. In the context of secondary education, the “head” is a system of shifting policy, endless accountability metrics, and top-down initiatives that routinely demand more from teachers without ever removing anything from their plates.

The most effective teachers are not those who work the longest hours; they are those who are demonstrably more effective in the classroom while protecting their cognitive and physical capacity. To survive and thrive in this profession, we must move away from martyrdom and embrace strategic, evidence-informed boundaries.
You do not need a novel starter, a complex group-work carousel, a tiered literacy task, and a creative plenary in every sixty-minute period. I am the first to admit I am sometimes guilty of this.

Instead of spending hours building a deck from a blank screen, take a well-sequenced resource created by another teacher or an online repository, and adapt your teaching around those slides. Sure, you might tweak a few numbers, add a diagnostic hinge question, or insert a quick mini-whiteboard check, but with practice, you can teach brilliantly off someone else’s framework.

It is infinitely better to walk into the classroom with four “good enough” lessons and a well-rested brain than to stay up until 2:00 a.m. crafting one “masterpiece” while stumbling through the other three in a state of sleep-deprived survival. Because you care about your craft, I can guarantee that your “imperfect” resources are nowhere near rubbish.

If your school asks you to embed extended discussions or vocabulary-heavy tasks, evaluate what it will cost in lesson time and cognitive focus. In mathematics, for example, procedural fluency and conceptual atomisation are foundational.
If you do not have the mental and physical energy to take on extra non-classroom duties, do not volunteer for them. Even during your timetabled duties, you must practice ruthless triage.

Educational systems will always expand to consume whatever time and energy you are willing to surrender to them. If you consistently sacrifice your evenings, your weekends, and your physical health to paper over structural cracks, nobody at the top will ever realise the foundation is failing.
